t: Lexicographically Smallest String After a Swap
o: We may swap at most one adjacent pair of digits sharing the same parity, aiming for the lexicographically smallest result. Greedy: scan left to right for the first position where s[i] > s[i+1] and both digits share parity — swapping there reduces the string at the earliest possible position, which dominates lexicographic order. If no such position exists, the string is already optimal.
k: Lexicographic order is decided at the earliest differing character, so improve the leftmost possible position.
A beneficial swap requires s[i] > s[i+1] AND same parity; the first such i gives the unique best answer.

a.i: Find the first index i with s[i] > s[i+1] and (s[i]-s[i+1]) even; perform that one swap and return. If none exists, return s unchanged.
s: On the first match, swap and return immediately.
a.t: O(n) — one pass with an immediate return on the first valid swap
a.sp: O(n) for the rebuilt string (O(1) extra in C++)

a.n: Approach 2: Try all candidate swaps and take the minimum
a.i: Generate every valid single swap (there are at most n-1) and return the lexicographic minimum. Simpler to reason about, still O(n²) which is trivial for n ≤ 100.
s: For each i with same-parity adjacent digits, form the swapped string.
Return the minimum over all candidates and s.
a.t: O(n²) — up to n candidate strings compared at O(n) each

w: Use the greedy scan in an interview; the enumeration version is a safe sanity check. Pitfall: the parity check applies to the digit values, not positions; also note a swap of equal digits is allowed but pointless. Edge cases: strictly increasing strings ("001") return unchanged, and "45320" shows the single swap at i=1. Follow-up: allow k swaps, or swaps of adjacent digits differing by at most d.
